Thank you, Nadar. It's a pleasure to be here in New York, High Level Week, and many people coming in through UN Web TV today. Let's jump right in with Ambassador Wallace. Thank you so much, Richard, and Nodara and colleagues. It's great to be here with you. Thanks to GGI and C4UN for convening such a timely discussion. I think for us to see some success, measurable success, from implementation of the Pact for the Future, we will need to have an ongoing process, similar to what civil society is doing, but an intergovernmental process that requires regular reporting and provision of feedback, so that member states are prepared for 2028 to bring the solutions, to bring the analysis that they have done for implementation and to bring the results of their implementation. Thank you so much, Ambassador, for, as you always do, providing solutions and not just identifying the crisis. Thank you. Thank you very much. And thank you also to the coalition, of course, the Stimson Center and the Permanent Mission of Namibia for convening this very timely discussion. The Pact for the Future was adopted at a moment of profound geopolitical division. So securing the agreement, I might say, under those conditions was itself quite an important achievement. But the context has not become easier. On the contrary, fragmentation has deepened, respect for common rules has become more selective, and the space for collective action has narrowed. So the pact must therefore be advanced under much more difficult conditions than those in which it was negotiated. But I do also want to remind ourselves that when the General Assembly took this decision, it was one country trying to interfere and try to not that the GA would not take that decision, but all the others said, no, we are going to do this. So there is a sense of urgency, I believe, among member states. We must also remember that the pact is not legally binding, and its adoption does not guarantee implementation. So, we must think of how to build trust, and this implementation will require political will, national ownership, and also sustained cooperation. And this matters for trust. Agreements do not restore confidence merely because they are adopted. Expectations followed by inaction can deepen cynicism. Trust will depend on whether people actually see the pact producing meaningful change by 2028. When President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and I co-chaired the Secretary-General's High-Level Advisory Board on Effective Multilateralism. We called for a breakthrough for people and planet, and we argued that multilateralism must be judged not on the number of declarations adopted, but instead by its capacity to manage shared risk, deliver global public goods, and involve those who are affected by its decision. Club de Madrid has strongly embraced global public goods as an organizing narrative that would be capable of holding this agenda together. Because at a time of rising nationalism and protectionism, they remind us that even where trust is scarce and values are contested, countries retain a shared interest in outcomes none can secure alone. From peace, pandemics, preparedness to climate and financial stability and other issues, they provide actually a practical foundation for rebuilding cooperation around common interests and tangible delivery. So over the next two years, I think three priorities are essential. First, Member States should now translate the Pact and its political commitments into clear national and international actions, with responsibility, with resources, timelines and measurable indicators. So, the 2028 review must be based on credible evidence of what has been achieved, and also where progress has stalled and why so. The second is that implementation must deliver results that people experience in their lives. Club de Madrid's Global Commission on Democracy and Multilateralism concludes that democracy and multilateralism face an interconnected crisis of trust, legitimacy, and delivery. So progress must therefore improve people's well-being, while of course protecting rights, participation, accountability and the rule of law. Third, the implementation must be inclusive. So we argue that parliaments, civil societies, young people, local authorities, affected communities need meaningful opportunities to influence decisions, not just consultation without consequence. And greater fairness among states and a stronger voice for the Global South are equally indispensable. Now, the arrival of our new Secretary-General offers an important opportunity to make Pact implementation a central priority, align the UN system behind achievable outcomes, and report publicly progress. But the Secretary-General cannot substitute for the political responsibility of Member States. Governments must provide the leadership that is necessary. And I want to underline two things here. The current Secretary-General has done a tremendous job in forming these processes, making these processes move forward. So we should thank him for that. And I also want to underline, it is the member states. It's always the members of an organization that makes what the organization is. So member states must step up here much, much better than we've seen so far. So by 2028, the question will not be whether the pact expressed the right ambitions. It will be whether member states choose to act on these. We know that trust cannot be requested, it must be earned through delivery, fairness, participation, and accountability. And there is an expectation of this pack. Just watch outside this building. When you come here, you can sense people want to come here. People see this as a very, very important venue to go to. So I think we should bring that with us going forward. Thank you.

Thank you, former Prime Minister Lofven, for your leadership over so many years. Next, we have Dr. Katarina Stasch. Thank you so much, Patel. I mean, Richard, first and foremost, thank you to you and the organizers for convening what I think is a really, really important conversation. And I think sometimes important to recognize that once we adopt these big things, really important to keep the conversation going, both on how we implement them, where do we get, what are the obstacles we meet on our way, and perhaps what are the sometimes the need for adjusting or finding sort of a different way around problems. I mean, I think on human rights, it's in many ways all in the opening, no? peoples. I mean, you cannot imagine the UN and the multilateral system without human rights there. But I think It's been said many times before, but of course, words are not enough. I think Pact for the Future in many ways set us on the path to recognizing the need to resource this commitment. It requested the Secretary-General to assess this need and ensure that there was sufficient funding also for the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. I have three points I want to make, and then I promise I'll make it at the end. The first is I really think that in the ongoing and never-ending discussion on UN reforms, and sometimes I think we shouldn't call it UN reform, but UN renewal, because that's actually what we need as much. And I think important that in this whole discussion around rationalization and efficiency, we don't end up cutting funding for the human rights pillar, which is already underfunded, because we will pay the price on so many other agendas. Second, and I think really, really important to remember and remind ourselves sometimes when you sit in this room, is that despite the mounting pressure on rights and democracy and freedoms, there remains an incredibly strong demand, popular demand for these things, for human rights, for democracy, for rule of law, accountable governance worldwide. And I think civil society plays an absolutely vital role in this respect, bringing that voice into these discussions. And civil society actors, now human rights defenders, of course, continue to look at the UN. They also look at the EU and many other member states, of course, in this room, to continue to stand up for these rights, but actually also to put them into practice. Now, my third point is, and I think, and you said it a little bit also, is let's also communicate and showcase also the many positive stories around multilateralism. And that also goes for the transformative power of human rights as an indispensable enabler of peace, of security, and of sustainable development. Let's not be swallowed by the doom and gloom. I think we really need to rally also the positive messages around multilateralism. And I think, so when we have the review next year, Let us not only focus on all the things that we did not manage to do, but let us also really shine a light on all the things that we managed to do. The promise is that the EU will remain a steadfast partner for all those who are seeking to build a world where justice, freedom, equality and human dignity are upheld for all. That's also why we support the Global Alliance for Human Rights, launched, I think, by the High Commissioner for Human Rights officially yesterday. And that's also why we are right now in the midst of preparing sort of our next seven-year action plan on human rights and democracy. Thank you so much, Ambassador. And thank you also for your leadership as permanent representative of Denmark during the negotiations as well. We really appreciate it. The fact that 56% of sub-actions indicators show some progress is encouraging, but the 30% showing no progress and 14% showing regression tell us that pledged commitments alone are not enough. The question is how Member States can turn this evidence into focused political action, because this commitment will not self-implement. So, three points. First, Member States need to put implementation and prevention at the center of multilateral agenda. Action 16 is a good illustration. The majority of this severance of actions, covert cooperation, mediation, peacemaking, and peaceful settlement of dispute, so minimum to no progress. Conflict escalation, repeated ceasefire violations, the growing role of non-state armed groups, and high military expenditures are placing enormous pressure on the international system and undermining confidence in international law. and the UN Charter. It's a bit encouraging that we met with the contenders for the position of the Secretary General, and all of them in the statement before the African Union at a meeting convened yesterday, show a commitment to, if and when elected, to push member states so that they put mediation at the central focus. Everybody talks about prevention, mediation, but you look at the commitment, you have Security Council, resolution 2719, for example, that commit resources to African peacekeeping operations. And people are clapping, and I clap along. But how much are the resources they're going to put into mediation and prevention? This is where to really talk about results, not just commitments. Also, member states can accelerate progress by championing the preventive diplomacy and good offices of the Secretary-General, developing national prevention strategies that are connected to existing national frameworks and affirming the peaceful settlement of disputes as a central commitment of the UN Charter. And this is important because progress on peace and prevention is an enabling condition for progress across the Pact and the 2030 Agenda. Conflict makes it much harder to advance development, protect human rights, address humanitarian needs, or achieve the SDGs. And again, I'm happy that this, the path and the 2030 agenda kind of resonates with the African Union, which as you know, African states are the biggest single block of nations, member states here. And their 2063 agenda is very much in line with this emphasis on mediation, prevention, and prevention. Second, member states need to address the financial gap. Action 4 and actions 47 through 52 on international financial architectural reform is fundamental to whether the pact and the SDGs can actually be implemented. The little reductions in development assistance, multilateral lending, and funding for international organization are constraining progress. The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026 makes the broader challenge clear. Only 36% of the 139 targets with trend data are on track or making moderate progress, while 49% are moving too slowly, and 15% have regressed below their 2015 benchmarks. I see one minute. Well, so I've just kind of give you the headlines. So, member states should scale up concessional and multilateral development financing, including increase regional development bank lending capacities, and mobilize private sector funding for the SDGs. Member states should also build directly on successful recent multilateral outcomes, such as FfB4, to further strategic non-governmental convening. Third and lastly, because I respect the sign, one minute, right? Third, we need to use monitoring to focus political attention, not simply to measure progress, but to draw attention to where we are falling behind. And finally, because the Pact innovation forums work, we know where progress is happening, we know where it is stalled, and increasingly, we know where it is going backwards. So, the task now for Member States is to translate that evidence into political priorities, mobilizing financing, strengthening prevention and peace making, and concentrating partnership and innovation where they can have the greatest impact. And this is where we have to mobilize civil society, NGOs, think tanks, including like mine, because governments don't act often except with prodding. And we have to work with those who actually influence from behind. And also make sure that private sector actually becomes partners, because of course, we have to make it clear to the private sector that without peace, which is the primary focus of this organization, they will not be able to make their profit. And the true business of business is to stay in business.

Thank you, Professor Ghamari, your legendary leadership here at the United Nations over decades. We asked our panelists to involve in a lightning round, 30-second responses. So climate change will hit the Mediterranean region among the hardest, for instance. So, thank you very much.
